title: Indicators of capacity and inflation pressures for Canada
summary: The Bank of Canada publishes a comprehensive data dashboard tracking capacity and inflation pressures across six categories: inflation, product market conditions, labour market, wages and costs, real estate market, and expectations. Latest data shows CPI inflation at 1.8% in February 2026 (within target), output gaps ranging from -0.8% to -1.6% across different methodologies, unemployment at 6.7%, and wage growth (LFS-Micro) moderating to 2.6% year-over-year in February.
key_points: CPI inflation stood at 1.8% in February 2026, within the Bank of Canada's 1-3% target band
Core inflation measures (CPI-trim at 2.3%, CPI-median at 2.3%, CPI-common at 2.4%) suggest underlying price pressures are contained
Output gap estimates range from -0.8% to -1.6%, indicating modest economic slack across different methodologies
Unemployment rate was 6.7% in February 2026, with labour market indicator at 6.7 and participation rate declining to 64.9%
Wage growth has been moderating: LFS average hourly earnings up 2.6% year-over-year in February, down from 4.9% in Q3 2024
Business survey data shows 24% of firms expect CPI inflation above 3% over the next six months, down from 45% in Q1 2025
Office vacancy rate remains elevated at 16.2% in Q4, while industrial vacancy rose to 5.5%
why_it_matters: This dashboard provides the key inputs the Bank of Canada uses to assess the output gap and inflation pressures when setting monetary policy. Traders and analysts monitor these indicators to gauge whether the BoC has room to cut rates or whether capacity constraints might push inflation above target. The combination of negative output gaps, moderating wages on some measures, and contained core inflation supports a backdrop where the BoC can maintain or ease policy without reigniting price pressures.
macro_context: The data presents a mixed picture for Canada: CPI inflation is near the 2% target and core measures are contained, while negative output gaps indicate economic slack. However, non-energy commodity prices have surged 19.4% year-over-year, which could eventually feed into broader inflation if sustained. Elevated office vacancies (16.2%) reflect lingering commercial real estate stress, and wage pressures vary by measure (LFS-Micro at 2.6% vs standard LFS at 3.9%), suggesting uneven labour market cooling.

issues_found: Wage growth misattributed: summary says 'LFS average hourly earnings up 2.6% year-over-year' but 2.6% is the LFS-Micro figure; the Labour Force Survey Average Hourly Earnings shows 3.9% in February 2026
Event type is 'unknown' which is technically correct for a data dashboard page but does not help with archival categorization
Non-energy commodity price index at 19.4% is correctly cited but could benefit from more context about its limited direct pass-through to CPI

human_review.notes: The record is mostly accurate and well-sourced, but contains a specific misattribution in the summary regarding wage growth data. The LFS-Micro figure (2.6%) is correct but should not be labeled as 'LFS average hourly earnings' when that label in the source refers to a different series showing 3.9%. This requires human correction to avoid misleading readers.

notes: This is a reference data page, not a market-moving event. The page compiles six categories of capacity and inflation indicators that the Bank of Canada uses to inform policy decisions. It serves as macro context rather than a catalyst. The next update is scheduled for April 29, 2026. Data appears current as of February 2026 (most series). Some series have longer lags (e.g., GDP chain price indices through Q4 2025). Source trust tier is high (bankofcanada.ca).
